items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the function [MATH: y=f(x)] whose graph is shown below. How can we plot the graph of [MATH: y=f(-x)?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/04708393fb4e5ed1e7af41c27a7a3d8e]

Content:
We can use some points on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] to find the corresponding points on the graphs of [MATH: y=f(-x).]

Content:
For example, let's take the point [MATH: (3,4)]. The fact that it's on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] means [MATH: f(3)=4.] Then, if [MATH: x={\color{red}-3},] we have

Content:
[MATH: f(-x) = f\left(-({\color{red}-3})\right) = f(3) = 4.]

Content:
This means the point [MATH: ({\color{red}3},4)] that lies on [MATH: y=f(x)] has a corresponding point [MATH: ({\color{red}-3},4)] that lies on [MATH: y=f(-x).]

Content:
So, for each point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x),] there will be a point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(-x)] with the same [MATH: y]-value and the opposite [MATH: x]-value:

Content:
[MATH: Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]|Points on [math]y=f(-x)[/math]; (− 1, 2)|(1, 2); (0, − 1)|(0, − 1); (2, 0)|(− 2, 0); (3, 4)|(− 3, 4)]

Content:
Finally, we can plot the points and draw the graph of [MATH: y = f(-x){:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/91ac272c761235cef7f263d7dcd332b7]

Content:
Looking back at the graph, we see that every point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(-x)] is the reflection across the [MATH: y]-axis of a point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x).]

Content:
So, the graph of [MATH: y=f(-x)] can be obtained by reflecting the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] over the [MATH: y]-axis. This result holds in general.

sections.normalized_html: The point [MATH: P] with coordinates [MATH: (1, 2)] lies on the curve [MATH: y=f(x).] Find a point that must lie on the graph of [MATH: y= f(-x).]
sections.readable_text: The point [MATH: P] with coordinates [MATH: (1, 2)] lies on the curve [MATH: y=f(x).] Find a point that must lie on the graph of [MATH: y= f(-x).]

sections.normalized_html:
The transformation [MATH: y=f(-x)] reflects the curve [MATH: y=f(x)] in the [MATH: y]-axis.

First, notice that the point [MATH: P(1, 2)] lies [MATH: 1] unit to the right of the [MATH: y]-axis. So, after the transformation is applied and the point is reflected across the [MATH: y]-axis, this point will lie [MATH: 1] unit to the left of the [MATH: y]-axis.

Therefore, the point [MATH: P'(-1, 2)] must lie on the graph of [MATH: y=f(-x).]
